newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian euthanasia families plea for law to stay.
newsitem.headline: Australian euthanasia families plea for law to stay.

text.p: The families of two people who died under the world's only assisted suicide law made an emotional last-ditch plea to parliament on Thursday to let dying Australians keep the right to kill themselves.

With parliament's upper house Senate due to decide the law's fate on Monday, the widow of the first person to die under the law begged politicians not to overturn "the most compassionate piece of legislation in the whole world".
And the widower of the second person to use the law said it allowed his terminally-ill wife to die with peace and dignity.
"Any of the senate that could have seen my wife in her condition, I'm sure they wouldn't have walked away ... without tears in their eyes," said David Mills.
Mills' wife, Janet, dying of a rare skin cancer, committed assisted suicide in January.

The Senate is expected on Monday to narrowly pass a bill killing off the controversial law. The bill was introduced by backbencher Kevin Andrews, member of a Christian morals faction within Prime Minister John Howard's Liberal Party.

Judy Dent, whose husband Bob was the first to use the law when he died in September after a computer-delivered fatal injection, said senators should heed the views of the vast majority of Australians who support euthanasia.

"I've decided to speak now because I'm afraid that the Senate is going to vote in favour of the Andrews bill, which will wipe out the most compassionate piece of legislation in the whole world," Dent told Australian radio.

The bill calls on the government to use its constitutional powers over Australia's territories to quash the law which came into effect in the remote Northern Territory last July. It has already received a clear majority in the lower house.
But the national government does not have the same power over Australia's six largely autonomous states and pro-euthansia campaigners say the fight will go on.
"We are hoping that if the Andrews bill unfortunately got through, that another state would pick up the ball," said leading euthanasia campaigner Dr Robert Marr.
"It's not going to stop euthanasia in Australia -- as a doctor, I know it goes on every day in our hospitals."

The Liberal leader of Victoria state, Jeff Kennett, has been one of the few political leaders to speak out strongly in support of euthanasia and euthanasia groups hope he would act if the territory law is quashed.
Mills, citing opinion polls showing 75 percent of Australians back the right to die, urged a national popular vote on the issue to take it out of politicians' hands.
"I think it's (the) only honest thing that should happen," he told reporters in Canberra, where he is lobbying senators in the final days before the vote
Four people have died using the law, which has been condemned by church, political and Aboriginal leaders.
"I am here today just to try and help the people of Australia that want to use this euthanasia law," said Mills.

"I think my wife would have liked me to do this even though its pretty hard. It would be a terrible shame if this bill was passed ... for all the people out there that really need to use this or want the right to be able to use the law."
